transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-18
Start time: 14:00 PT
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Alex (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Mark (Pioneer CTO), Jenna (Head of ML), Omar (SRE), Claire (Finance)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be rough):
Pioneer is evaluating Redwood for a customer-facing chat summarization product. Primary concerns: unit economics per token, latency targets for a live chat (under 400ms p50 for short prompts), and whether Dedicated or Private deployment is needed given data residency and long-term volume. They asked detailed questions about batching, KV/prefix caching, quantization tradeoffs and how Redwood's routing/fallbacks affect per-token cost. Next steps agreed: pricing spreadsheet and one-week POC benchmark.

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, um we're excited to learn about Pioneer. I think we have about 40 minutes. Quick intros?
[00:08] Mark: Hi I'm Mark Rivera, CTO, I run infra and platform here at Pioneer. We build a multi-tenant chat assistant, heavy summarization and retrieval augmented generation.
[00:15] Jenna: Jenna, Head of ML, focusing on model ranking and prompt engineering.
[00:18] Omar: Omar, SRE, I'm mostly worried about cost and operational limits.
[00:22] Claire: Claire, finance, I'll be looking at unit economics and procurement.
[00:26] Alex: Cool. Priya is our SE, she'll dig into performance and batching later.
[00:30] Priya: Hi all — quick agenda, a few Qs around your workload/volume, then we'll go into cost breakdowns and deployment options.

[00:40] Mark: High level, we expect 2–3M tokens/day initially, ramping to 25–30M within 6 months. Latency targets: under 400ms p50 for short chat replies, p90 under 800ms. We're also looking at peak spikes of 200 QPS. Budget is tight — finance looking for <$15k/month initially for inference if possible.

[01:05] Alex: Ok that's helpful. Question on the 15k/mo — is that total infra spend or just the LLM API spend?
[01:10] Claire: Just LLM API spend — other infra is separate.
[01:14] Alex: Got it. Quick note — our hosted API pricing depends on model choice and tokens. For example, our mid-tier open models are priced around $0.003 per 1k input tokens and $0.006 per 1k output tokens as a list price; we can work with committed spend for discounts.

[01:40] Jenna: Can you unpack what drives that delta? How much is kernel/hardware vs software features like batching and caching?
[01:48] Priya: Yeah — good question. Roughly the main levers are raw compute time (GPU cycles), batching efficiency, and cache hit-rate. On-hosted we meter per-token for the full request/response; but if you move to Dedicated you can get better amortization: larger batch sizes, longer KV-cache reuse, and you avoid multi-tenant overhead. Practically we've seen customers cut effective per-token cost by 30–60% when moving from small hosted usage to dedicated pools with autoscaling and caching tuned.

[02:20] Omar: So what's realistic for us — 3M tokens/day at start. If we do hosted and assume average prompt:completion ratio 1:2, that's 9M tokens/month. At $0.006 per 1k completion tokens + $0.003 per 1k prompt tokens how does that map?
[02:40] Alex: Quick math, rough: 9M tokens/month is 9000 units of 1k. If half are completions (this depends on ratio), at those list prices that's like $27 to $54 a month wait that doesn't sound right, hold on — let me re-calc. (laughter)
[02:58] Alex: Ok sorry scratch that, let me be precise: If you have 9M tokens, that's 9000 * 1k. Prompts at $0.003 per 1k => $27. Completions at $0.006 per 1k => $54. Total ~ $81/month raw API invoice at list pricing — that seems low — so maybe our numbers are per 1k for thousand tokens yes this is why we must be careful, many customers measure in millions so check your monthly totals.
[03:28] Jenna: Hmm that seems low compared to our expectation. Our earlier estimate was more like $5k/mo for similar usage. Are we missing something like model size multiplier or context length?
[03:36] Priya: Right — two important things: 1) those list prices are for our smaller opt models; if you use a larger 70B or LLM variant the compute multiplier increases — e.g., a 70B family could be 4–8x the price of a small opt model. 2) Tokenization and context windows matter — if you have long chat histories your effective tokens per call goes up. Also embedding and reranking calls are priced differently.
[04:00] Mark: For us typical context is 1.5k tokens in, 250 tokens out average. Prompts are heavy.
[04:08] Priya: With 1.5k in + 250 out, each call is 1.75k tokens. If you have 100k calls a month that's 175M tokens. At 175k units of 1k tokens, at $0.003 per prompt-unit that's $525 and completions at $0.006 adds another $1050 — total ~ $1.6k/mo at those list prices for small models. But scale and model family could push that to $6–8k/mo.
[04:44] Claire: That aligns more with our finance expectations. So main question: can batching and prefix caching materially lower our effective cost?
[04:53] Priya: Yes. Two levers you'll use: 1) batching — if your clients can tolerate slightly higher latency you can increase batch window and drive GPU utilization up, which reduces per-token compute. 2) KV/prefix caching — for repeated prefixes or system prompts, KV cache avoids recomputing initial layers and reduces work per token for subsequent calls. For a conversational product with a lot of repeated system tokens we've seen effective per-token cost drop by ~20–40% with caching.

[05:23] Omar: How about quantization — are you doing int8 or int4 in Hosted? Does that affect latency?
[05:30] Priya: We support quantized variants. Hosted exposes curated quantized models that trade a bit of quality for throughput/cost. Dedicated and Private give you more control — you can run int8/int4 kernels depending on model. Quantization can reduce memory and increase batch sizes; latency per token often improves slightly, but the main win is fitting larger models on cheaper hardware so unit cost drops.
[05:56] Mark: If we care about p50 under 400ms what's the recommended path? Hosted or Dedicated?
[06:02] Priya: For strict p50 of <400ms on moderate sizes (~70B) Dedicated is usually the recommended approach — fewer noisy neighbors, pinned GPUs, bespoke batching strategy. Hosted can hit <400ms for smaller models or warmed instances with caching, but it's less predictable under peak spikes unless you commit to a higher tier or burst capacity.
[06:24] Jenna: Can you give an example of a committed reserved contract price delta? Like what does Dedicated cost compared to Hosted per 1k tokens at scale?
[06:33] Alex: Numbers vary by commitment. A rough example: at $100k/month committed throughput, effective per-1k token might be 40–60% lower than list hosted prices because you amortize the GPU and get higher batching. So if hosted is $0.006/completion, dedicated effective could be $0.002–0.003 per 1k on similar model family.
[06:57] Claire: That's the level we need to see to hit budget. Do you have an example calc for our projected 175M tokens/month?
[07:05] Priya: If we take 175M tokens = 175k * 1k. At hosted list for small model family: prompts $0.003 = $525; completions $0.006 = $1,050 => $1,575. For a larger heavier model family multiply by 4x => ~$6.3k. With Dedicated at committed rates you could be down to $2k–$3k for that same workload. But exact numbers need model choice and commitment window.
[07:32] Mark: Ok good. Another question: how do autoscaling and burst capacity factor into cost and SLOs? If we keep reserved capacity but get a flash spike, is there an automatic fallback to hosted?
[07:44] Alex: Yes — Redwood supports smart routing and automatic fallback to hosted capacity or different model variants. You can configure policies: keep p50/p90 on dedicated up to X, then fall back to hosted cheaper models or degraded latency/quality. Fallback usage can be metered differently. We'll show options in the pricing spreadsheet.
[08:04] Omar: On security — we will likely need Private/VPC because of PII and data residency. How different is cost for Private compared to Dedicated?
[08:13] Priya: Private has an upfront platform fee and additional ops costs; per-token serving costs are similar to Dedicated but you also cover networking and optional on-prem infra. Typically Private suits regulated customers where compliance matters; Dedicated is a simpler step if you can accept managed environment and dedicated GPU pools.
[08:34] Jenna: For the POC — what are typical benchmarks you run? We care about throughput (QPS), tokens/sec, and p50/p90 latency.
[08:42] Priya: We'll run a 1-week POC where we: 1) onboard your prompt set, 2) run a traffic replay at target QPS with synthetic user noise, 3) measure p50/p90 latencies and effective per-token cost under different batching and cache configs, 4) provide a cost breakdown and recommendation whether hosted/dedicated/private. We'll need sample prompts and an expected QPS profile.
[09:06] Mark: We'll provide that. For the POC do you require shipping data to Redwood? We're trying to avoid external PII transfer.
[09:14] Alex: You can use anonymized or synthetic traffic for benchmarks. If you need to test with real data, Private deployment is the way to go. We'll also sign an NDA and discuss DPA clauses.
[09:26] Claire: On billing — do you invoice monthly or can you do a committed monthly charge against which usage is reconciled?
[09:33] Alex: We do both. Hosted is typically usage-based monthly billing. Dedicated has commitment/recurring invoices and we reconcile overages or credits. We'll put standard terms in the quote.
[09:44] Jenna: A quick question on prefix caching — how often do cache hits happen for conversational assistants? Our turns vary and users have distinct contexts.
[09:52] Priya: It depends — for system prompts and common templates hits can be high. For user-specific context it's lower. One pattern is to split prompts: keep long immutable system/context cached while streaming recent tokens; that gets you the benefits without losing per-user context. In practice customers with high reuse see 10–30% reduction in compute from caching.
[10:12] Mark: What about combined effects — batching plus caching plus quantization — can we get up to 60% reduction?
[10:18] Priya: Yes that's in the upper bound we've seen: quant + cache + aggressive batching on dedicated infra yields 40–60% effective cost cut relative to naive hosted calls. But you tradeoff latency and in some cases a bit of output quality.
[10:30] Omar: For the pilot, can we instrument token-level cost so finance can map to our internal chargeback?
[10:35] Alex: Absolutely — Console gives token-level and route-level breakdowns, per-route dashboards, and exportable cost reports. We can map keys to your internal project tags.
[10:44] Claire: Who are the stakeholders for a decision? I need to coordinate procurement and legal.
[10:49] Mark: Decision makers: me (CTO) for architecture, Jenna for model selection, Claire for finance, and VP of Product (not on call) will sign off. Timeline: we want vendor selection within 6 weeks.
[11:03] Alex: Great. Two quick clarifications — is data residency US only or EU as well?
[11:08] Mark: EU customers are important — need EU data residency for some accounts.
[11:12] Priya: We have region options; Dedicated/private can host in specific cloud regions. We'll call out options in security pack.
[11:20] Jenna: Any gotchas on egress costs for Private?
[11:24] Priya: If you run on-prem you'll manage network egress. For VPC/private cloud deployments we help estimate egress and it can be included in the quote.
[11:32] Alex: Ok wrapping up — recap of next steps: we'll send a pricing and commitment worksheet that shows Hosted list price vs Dedicated committed examples and a modeled calc for your 175M token scenario with optimistic/pessimistic model families; Priya will prepare a POC plan; Jenna to share sample prompts and QPS profile; Claire to share target budget constraints.
[11:53] Mark: Sounds good. One last quick thing — competitors: we've talked to OpenAI for hosted and to a couple infra vendors like Run:ai for dedicated orchestration. Key decision criteria: predictability of cost, having a single SLA across environments, and observability.
[12:10] Alex: We'll include observability screenshots and the Console export in the packet.
[12:14] Claire: Procurement will need standard SOX-ish terms — can you share contract templates?
[12:18] Alex: Yes we'll share master services agreement and DPA.
[12:21] Jenna: Thanks everyone, we'll look for the docs and the POC plan.
[12:26] Priya: I'll follow up with the benchmark steps and a checklist for what we need from you.
[12:30] Alex: Thanks all — meeting end.

Notes on transcription errors / noise: speaker overlap at times, some model names were abbreviated (70B family referenced as '70 bee' at one point), 'KV cache' sometimes transcribed as 'K V cache' or 'keevy cache'. Numbers were approximated during call and follow up doc will contain canonical pricing.
